description: We’re Math 1007, an Ottawa team interested in math, coding, and space exploration. We’re excited to brainstorm, learn from each other, and build something together at NASA Space Apps. We’d love to connect with people who enjoy programming, design, research, or explaining ideas clearly. Beginners are welcome!
summary:
Lunar Life is a pixel-art game that trains kids aged 7–12 to be junior astronauts. They live at a research outpost near the Moon’s South Pole for a five-day mission. Players train first at an astronaut academy: they suit up, practice spacewalk repairs in a training pool and catch cargo with a robotic arm. On the Moon they run the outpost, balancing a solar battery through long shadows, growing food without soil and spotting flares on a sun-cam. They also learn why a message to Earth takes time to arrive.

On the last day, a solar particle storm hits, replayed from NASA’s real DONKI record of May 10, 2024. Players must rush the crew into a shielded shelter and choose what to power while they wait. A mission report rates their choices for crew safety, power and food, and explains why each outcome happened.

Every activity teaches one real fact by doing it. Collectible field notes link each fact to its NASA source. Lunar Life makes the real trade-offs of living on the Moon something kids can feel, not just read about.
details:
What it does
Lunar Life is a pixel-art game where kids aged 7 to 12 become junior astronauts on a five-day mission at a research outpost near the Moon’s South Pole.

  • Day 1, academy training. Players suit up in the right order, practice spacewalk repairs in a training pool, catch cargo with a robotic arm, and learn to manage power before a long shadow.
  • Days 2 to 4, life at the outpost. Players check the solar battery each morning and grow food in plant pillows under coloured LED lights. They run a light experiment, tell moon dust (regolith) apart from soil, and keep their bones strong on the exercise bike. They also watch the Sun for flares and send a message to Earth to see the communication delay.
  • Day 5, the storm. A solar particle event arrives. Players rush the crew into the shielded shelter by holding E to crank open the heavy hatch, then choose what the outpost powers while they wait.
  • Mission report. It shows a battery chart of the whole shift and star ratings for crew safety, power, and food and science, and explains in plain language why each result happened.

How it works

  • Three core resources link every decision: power, radiation shielding and food. Choices carry over from day to day, so habits matter on storm day.
  • The storm replays a real NASA DONKI solar energetic particle record from May 10, 2024. We label it honestly as an archived record detected near Earth, not a dose measured on the Moon.
  • Every activity teaches one real fact by doing it. A “Why” line comes before each activity and a “You learned” line after it.
  • Collectible field notes give each real fact, explain how the game simplifies it, and link the NASA page it comes from.

Benefits and intended impact
Kids don’t just read that mass blocks radiation or that batteries run down in the shadow. They feel it through their own decisions. Failing is safe and always comes with a hint, and replaying with a different strategy gives a different outcome. Our goal is for players to remember the science because they did it with their own hands, and to see real NASA data and space careers as something within their reach.

Creativity

  • Each lesson is a short hands-on minigame instead of a quiz, like filling a wick water tank “not too much, not too little” or tightening bolts while floating.
  • The radiation storm is built on real space weather data and ends in a genuine trade-off, not a free choice.
  • All the art, sound and music are original. Our own scripts paint the rooms, and the sounds and music are synthesized in code.

Tools and technology

  • Godot 4.7 with GDScript, in 480×270 pixel art with integer scaling.
  • Python (NumPy, Pillow) for the art painters and audio synthesis.
  • SpriteCook for the astronaut sprite animations.
  • NASA DONKI space weather data, saved in the game.
  • The Galmuri pixel font (SIL Open Font License).
  • Git and GitHub for teamwork, plus an automated playtest that plays the whole game and runs over 300 checks.

Factors we considered

  • Age-appropriate language: short dialogue boxes, everyday words, and a quick explanation for every science term.
  • Scientific honesty: we say clearly what is real and what is simplified.
  • Accessibility: keyboard and gamepad support, readable pixel text, and meaning that never relies on colour alone.
  • Balance: three resources instead of six, so the trade-offs stay clear.
  • Pacing: every story screen waits for the player instead of auto-advancing.
